claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with Mg distributed homogeneously in the matrix.
High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing environment accelerates decomposition of the metastable solid solution.
The Mg-rich intermetallic compounds form preferentially along grain boundaries and also within the matrix.
Mg-rich intermetallic formation disrupts the integrity of the protective oxide film.
Disruption of the protective oxide film decreases corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
Disruption of the protective oxide film decreases high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Thermally activated Mg diffusion causes Mg segregation and intermetallic-phase formation.
Oxide-scale formation creates or increases local compositional gradients.
Oxide-scale-driven compositional gradients facilitate the coarsening and networking of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Oxidizing treatment produces a more continuous network of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds than is present in the initial state.
At the same thermal profile, transformation under an inert atmosphere is slower or less pronounced than under an oxidizing atmosphere.
Inert-treated samples retain more corrosion and oxidation resistance than oxidizing-treated samples.
The proposed transformation and property degradation occur over approximately 600–800 °C and 10–50 hours.
At lower temperatures or very short exposure times, kinetics may be insufficient to produce appreciable Mg segregation and intermetallic formation.
Minor elemental additions or small compositional changes may alter the kinetics and spatial distribution of Mg-rich phases.
